newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais strong performance lifts shares.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais strong performance lifts shares.

text.p: Investors drove up shares in Credit Lyonnais more than seven percent on Friday after the state-controlled French bank delivered earnings results for last year that exceeded market expectations.

The bank, which nearly collapsed earlier in the decade under the weight of its lending excesses, reported late Thursday a modest net profit but a vastly improved underlying performance, fuelling hopes its recovery would be quicker than anticipated .
Shares, which account for 20 percent of the bank's capital but do not carry voting rights, closed up 7.37 percent at 204 francs after analysts upgraded profit forecasts.
The net profit rise to 202 million francs from 13 million matched forecasts but underlying figures were "better than expected on the quality side," said John Leonard of Salomon.

"One has the feeling Credit Lyonnais can rebound," said Transbourse analyst Patrick Leguil. He switched his rating on the share to "buy" from "sell", citing the bank's strong rise in operating profit, and cost control, among other factors.
Operating profit soared 42 percent to 9.5 billion and pretax, pre-exceptional profit tripled to 4.5 billion.
The bank, which the government plans privatise by 1999 after giving it another dose of public money to boost its balance sheet, forecast 1997 net profit in the "billions" of francs.

EIFB analyst Sami Gotrane said the figures showed the bank accelerated its recovery in the 1996 second half. While he did not believe a newspaper report last month that the bank expected a 1997 net profit of 3-4-3.7 billion francs, he said it would likely be "far higher than two billion".

Bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade said on Friday the bank would need to be recapitalised to boost its solvency ratios to acceptable levels to be privatised. But he said the government would get all of the money back -- and more -- when it sells it.
"The revenue from the privatisation will much higher than the recapitalisation" and the impact on public finances "will be positive," Peyrelevade told the daily Le Monde.
The government, which has provided financial life support to the bank since it plunged heavily into loss in 1992, is expected to have to pump at least 10 billion francs into the bank.

In addition to raising solvency ratios, the money will be needed to offset capital losses on asset sales expected to be demanded by European Commision in exchange for approving the newest aid package -- the third in four years.

But getting money back from the recapitalisation will not make a big dent in the massive final bill to the state from saving the bank. That cost includes 102 billion francs of losses expected from sales of dud assets spun off into a state-backed holding company under a 1995 government rescue.
Peyrelevade said the bank would continue to reduce its balance sheet to meet European Commission conditions for the bailout of the bank but said there would be no fire sales.
He envisaged the bank -- whose ill-fated expansion drive briefly made it the largest bank outside Japan -- returning to the size it was in 1998 "before the crazy period started".
Peyrelevade, who steered the recovery, said the bank would be "viable, profitable and able to privatised" in 1998 or 1999.

He acknowledged the bank's strong performance might further dismay rivals who complain taxpayers have paid for its recovery. But he said he had no intention of seeing the bank dismantled as demanded by Societe Generale chairman Marc Vienot.
"I will not accept a second destruction of Credit Lyonnais."
